title: A Hundred Prisoners, A Hundred Boxes
statement: $100$ numbered prisoners must each find their own number among $100$ closed boxes. The boxes hold the numbers $1$ to $100$ in a uniformly random arrangement. One at a time, each prisoner may open $50$ boxes, then leaves without communicating. Everyone is freed only if every prisoner finds their number. Before starting they may agree on a strategy. Using the optimal strategy, what is their probability of success? (Give a decimal.)
insight: Each prisoner opens their own box and then follows the numbers inside. Everyone succeeds exactly when the permutation has no cycle longer than 50.
redHerring: Assuming independence gives (1/2)^100. The point is to make the prisoners' successes and failures happen together.
hints: Random guessing gives $(1/2)^{100}$. You want the prisoners to succeed or fail together.
Treat the boxes as a permutation: box $i$ points to the number inside it. Start at your own box and keep following.
Following from your own box, you find your number within the length of your cycle. When does everyone succeed? Count permutations with a cycle longer than 50.
solution:
Prisoner $i$ opens box $i$, then the box whose number they just saw, and so on. They are walking around the cycle that contains $i$, so they find $i$ within 50 steps iff that cycle has length $\le 50$. Everyone succeeds iff the permutation has no cycle longer than 50.

At most one cycle can be longer than 50. The number of permutations of $n=100$ with a cycle of length $k>50$ is $\binom{n}{k}(k-1)!(n-k)! = \tfrac{n!}{k}$, so the probability of such a cycle is $\tfrac1k$.

$P(\text{success}) = 1 - \sum_{k=51}^{100}\tfrac1k \approx 1 - \ln 2 \approx 0.3118$. This strategy is known to be optimal.
